Reading links were checked on 2026-10-02. Diagrams are mermaid flowcharts rendered client-side with securityLevel 'strict'.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.goal: Agree on what to build and what 'good' means before drawing anything.
checklist: List 3-5 core functional requirements; park the rest out loud
Ask about scale: DAU, read/write ratio, data size, regions
Pin the non-functionals: latency target, availability, consistency, durability
Write assumptions down where the interviewer can see them

steps.title: Back-of-the-envelope
steps.goal: Turn scale into QPS, storage and bandwidth so the design has numbers to defend.
checklist: QPS = daily requests / 86,400 (≈ 10^5 s); peak ≈ 2-3× average
Storage = items/day × size × retention × replication factor
Bandwidth = QPS × payload size
Say which number drives the design (e.g. reads ≫ writes → cache)

steps.title: API
steps.goal: Define the contract the clients use; it fixes the scope of the rest.
checklist: 3-6 endpoints or RPCs with inputs and outputs
Pagination (cursor), idempotency keys on writes, auth
Sync vs async: which calls return 202 and finish later

steps.title: Data model
steps.goal: Choose entities, keys and the store that fits the access pattern.
checklist: Entities and their primary/partition keys
Access patterns first, then SQL vs NoSQL vs blob vs search
Indexes, and how the largest table is partitioned

steps.title: High-level design
steps.goal: Draw the boxes that satisfy every functional requirement end to end.
checklist: Client → edge (DNS/CDN/LB) → stateless services → data stores
Walk one write path and one read path through the diagram
Add queues where work can be async; caches where reads dominate

steps.title: Deep dives & trade-offs
steps.goal: Go deep on the 2-3 hardest parts and name what you'd trade.
checklist: Bottlenecks and hot spots: hot keys, celebrity users, fan-out
Failure modes: what happens when each box dies; retries, idempotency
Consistency choices and why; what you'd monitor (SLOs, alerts)

latency.label: Round trip in the same data centre

rubric.label: Clarified requirements and wrote down what's out of scope
Estimated QPS, storage and bandwidth, and used them in a decision
Defined a clear API including pagination and idempotency
Picked stores from access patterns and explained partition keys
High-level diagram covers every functional requirement end to end
Found the real bottleneck (hot key, fan-out, write amplification…) and fixed it
Covered failure modes: retries, timeouts, replicas, degraded mode
Named trade-offs explicitly (consistency vs latency, cost vs freshness…)
Mentioned observability: metrics, SLOs, alerts, dashboards
Finished inside 45 minutes with time for deep dives

blocks.name: Load balancer
blocks.summary: Spreads requests across stateless servers and removes unhealthy ones.
tradeoffs: L4 is fast and protocol-agnostic; L7 can route by path/header and retry, but costs more CPU
Sticky sessions simplify state but unbalance load and break on failover
blocks.pitfall: Forgetting the LB itself needs redundancy (active-passive pair or managed LB) and health checks that test real dependencies, not just a 200 from /.

blocks.name: Cache (Redis / Memcached)
blocks.summary: Keeps hot data in memory to cut read latency and database load.
tradeoffs: Cache-aside is simple but serves stale data until TTL or invalidation
Write-through keeps the cache fresh at the cost of write latency
More memory vs lower hit rate
blocks.pitfall: Cache stampede when a hot key expires: use request coalescing, jittered TTLs or early refresh. And never cache private data in a shared layer.

blocks.name: CDN
blocks.summary: Serves static and cacheable content from edge locations near users.
tradeoffs: Pull CDNs are easy but the first request misses; push gives control but you manage uploads
Long TTLs are cheap but invalidation is slow
blocks.pitfall: Bad cache keys: including cookies or random query params destroys the hit rate. Version asset URLs instead of purging.

blocks.name: Message queue / log (Kafka, SQS)
blocks.summary: Decouples producers from consumers so slow or failing work doesn't block requests.
tradeoffs: Kafka keeps an ordered, replayable log per partition; SQS-style queues are simpler but don't replay
At-least-once delivery means consumers must be idempotent
blocks.pitfall: Ordering only holds within a partition: choose the partition key (user id, order id) so related events stay together.

blocks.name: Sharding (partitioning)
blocks.summary: Splits a dataset across nodes by a key so storage and writes scale horizontally.
useWhen: One node can't hold the data or the write rate
tradeoffs: Range partitioning supports scans but creates hot ranges; hash partitioning spreads load but loses range queries
Cross-shard joins and transactions get expensive
blocks.pitfall: A low-cardinality or skewed key (country, celebrity user) makes one shard hot. Plan resharding before you need it.

blocks.name: Replication
blocks.summary: Copies data to multiple nodes for availability, durability and read scaling.
useWhen: You can't lose data when a node dies
tradeoffs: Leader-follower is simple; async replicas can serve stale reads
Multi-leader and leaderless (quorum) raise availability but need conflict resolution
blocks.pitfall: Read-your-writes: a user writes to the leader and reads a lagging replica. Route their reads to the leader for a short window.

blocks.name: Consistent hashing
blocks.summary: Maps keys to nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys.
tradeoffs: Virtual nodes smooth the distribution but add metadata
Rendezvous hashing is simpler for small clusters
blocks.pitfall: Without virtual nodes a few physical nodes own huge arcs of the ring and become hot.

blocks.name: Rate limiting
blocks.summary: Caps requests per client per window to protect services and share capacity fairly.
tradeoffs: Token bucket allows bursts; sliding-window log is exact but memory-heavy; fixed windows are cheap but spiky at edges
Central counters (Redis) are accurate but add a hop; local limits are fast but approximate
blocks.pitfall: Non-atomic read-then-write counters race under load. Use INCR with expiry or a Lua script.

blocks.name: Search index (Elasticsearch / OpenSearch)
blocks.summary: Inverted index for full-text search, filtering and relevance ranking.
tradeoffs: Near-real-time, not transactional: index asynchronously from the source of truth
Great reads, costly writes and reindexing
blocks.pitfall: Using the search index as the primary database. Keep the DB as truth and rebuild the index from it (CDC).

blocks.name: Blob / object store (S3)
blocks.summary: Cheap, durable storage for large immutable objects like images, video and backups.
useWhen: Files larger than a few hundred KB
tradeoffs: Very durable and cheap, but higher latency than block storage
Strong read-after-write now, but no partial in-place updates
blocks.pitfall: Proxying uploads through your app servers. Hand clients pre-signed URLs and upload directly.

blocks.name: Observability
blocks.summary: Metrics, logs and traces that tell you whether the system meets its SLOs and why not.
useWhen: Always; mention it in every design
tradeoffs: High-cardinality metrics and full tracing are powerful but expensive; sample
Push vs pull metrics collection
blocks.pitfall: Alerting on causes (CPU 80%) instead of symptoms users feel (error rate, p99 latency against the SLO).

blocks.name: Unique ID generation
blocks.summary: Creates globally unique, ideally time-sortable IDs without a central bottleneck.
tradeoffs: Snowflake (time + machine + sequence) sorts by time but needs worker-id assignment and clock care
UUIDv4 is coordination-free but random (bad index locality); UUIDv7/ULID are time-ordered
blocks.pitfall: Clock skew or NTP jumps backwards can duplicate Snowflake IDs; refuse to issue IDs until the clock catches up.

cases.title: URL shortener (bit.ly)
cases.summary: Turn long URLs into short codes and redirect billions of clicks with low latency.
functional: Create a short URL for a long URL (optional custom alias and expiry)
Redirect a short URL to the original
nonFunctional: Codes must not collide; not easily guessable
estimates: 100M new URLs/month ≈ 40 writes/s; 100:1 reads ≈ 4k redirects/s, peak ~10k
5 years × 1.2B/yr = 6B URLs × 500 B ≈ 3 TB
7 Base62 chars = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, plenty
dataModel: urls(code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at) in a KV/wide-column store partitioned by code
clicks events → Kafka → aggregated counts per code per day
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Client"] --> LB["Load balancer"]
  LB --> API["Shortener API"]
  API --> KGS["Key generator"]
  API --> DB[("URL store")]
  LB --> R["Redirect service"]
  R --> C[("Redis cache")]
  C -. miss .-> DB
  R --> K["Kafka: clicks"]
  K --> AGG["Stream aggregator"]
  AGG --> ST[("Stats store")]

deepDives.title: Generating codes
deepDives.body: Hashing the URL (MD5 → first 7 Base62 chars) needs collision checks. A global counter encoded in Base62 is collision-free but predictable and a single point of failure. A key-generation service that pre-allocates ranges of IDs to each API node (or Snowflake IDs → Base62) gives uniqueness without a hot counter.

deepDives.title: 301 vs 302
deepDives.body: 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, cutting load but hiding repeat clicks from analytics. 302 keeps every click visible. Most shorteners use 302 when analytics matter.

deepDives.title: Read path
deepDives.body: Redirects dominate, so put a cache (Redis or CDN edge) in front of the store with a long TTL. The mapping is immutable, so invalidation only happens on delete/expiry.

deepDives.title: Analytics without slowing redirects
deepDives.body: Emit a click event asynchronously to Kafka and return the redirect immediately; aggregate per minute/day in a stream job.

tradeoffs: Counter vs hash vs KGS for codes
302 + analytics vs 301 + lower load
Strong uniqueness on create vs eventual consistency for stats
probes: How do you avoid two nodes issuing the same code?
What happens when a hot link goes viral?
How do you stop people enumerating codes?
How would you support custom aliases safely?

readings.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know
System Design Primer: Pastebin / shortener walkthrough

cases.title: Distributed key-value store (Dynamo)
cases.summary: A highly available, partitioned KV store with tunable consistency.
nonFunctional: Scale horizontally to hundreds of nodes
estimates: 10 TB data, RF=3 → 30 TB raw; ~100 nodes at 300 GB each
100k ops/s → ~1k ops/s per node
dataModel: Each node: LSM tree (memtable + SSTables + commit log)
Ring metadata: token → node, shared by gossip
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> CO["Coordinator node"]
  CO --> N1["Replica A"]
  CO --> N2["Replica B"]
  CO --> N3["Replica C"]
  N1 <-. gossip .-> N2
  N2 <-. gossip .-> N3
  N1 --> L1[("LSM storage")]
  N2 --> L2[("LSM storage")]
  N3 --> L3[("LSM storage")]

deepDives.title: Partitioning
deepDives.body: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes places each key on the ring; the next N distinct nodes clockwise hold replicas. Adding a node moves only its share of keys.

deepDives.title: Quorums
deepDives.body: With N replicas, writes wait for W acks and reads for R. R + W > N gives overlapping sets, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write. N=3, W=2, R=2 is the common balance.

deepDives.title: Failures
deepDives.body: Gossip spreads membership and suspicion. Sloppy quorum plus hinted handoff keeps writes flowing when a replica is down; read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy fix divergence later.

deepDives.title: Conflicts
deepDives.body: Concurrent writes produce siblings. Vector clocks detect them; resolve with last-write-wins (simple, loses data) or app-level merge (shopping cart union).

tradeoffs: Consistency vs availability per request (R/W)
LWW simplicity vs merge correctness
LSM write speed vs read/compaction cost
probes: What does R + W > N guarantee, exactly?
How does a node learn another is dead?
What is hinted handoff and when does it fail?
How do you rebalance when adding nodes?

readings.title: Dynamo: Amazon's highly available key-value store (paper)

cases.title: Distributed rate limiter
cases.summary: Limit requests per user/IP/API key across a fleet of gateways.
functional: Rules like 100 req/min per API key, 5 logins/min per IP
Return 429 with Retry-After and remaining-quota headers
nonFunctional: Accurate within a few percent under concurrency
Fail open if the limiter store is down (configurable)
estimates: 1M active keys × ~100 B state ≈ 100 MB in Redis
50k req/s → 50k Redis ops/s: one shard, or a few for headroom
dataModel: Redis key per (rule, client): token count + last refill time, with TTL
Rules in a config store cached in each gateway
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> GW["API gateway + limiter"]
  GW -- "Lua: take token" --> R[("Redis cluster")]
  GW -- allowed --> S["Backend services"]
  GW -- "429 + Retry-After" --> C
  CFG[("Rules config")] -. cached .-> GW

deepDives.title: Algorithms
deepDives.body: Token bucket (refill rate r, capacity b) allows bursts up to b; leaky bucket smooths output; fixed window is cheap but allows 2× at window edges; sliding-window log is exact but stores every timestamp; sliding-window counter approximates it with two buckets.

deepDives.title: Atomicity
deepDives.body: Read-modify-write from many gateways races. A Redis Lua script (or INCR + EXPIRE) makes take-a-token atomic in one round trip.

deepDives.title: Scale and latency
deepDives.body: Shard Redis by key. For very hot paths, keep a local token bucket per gateway that syncs with Redis periodically: approximate, but no network hop.

deepDives.title: Failure policy
deepDives.body: If Redis is unreachable, fail open for most APIs (availability) but fail closed for login/OTP endpoints (security).

tradeoffs: Exactness vs memory (log vs counters)
Central accuracy vs local speed
Fail open vs fail closed
probes: How do you keep two gateways from both granting the last token?
Where does the limiter live: client, gateway, service?
How would you limit by multiple dimensions at once?
What headers do you return?

readings.title: Stripe: Scaling your API with rate limiters
Cloudflare: Counting things, a lot of different things
GitHub REST API rate limits (a real public contract)

cases.title: Unique ID generator (Snowflake)
cases.summary: Generate unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs at high rate without coordination.
functional: Return a unique 64-bit ID per call
IDs sort roughly by creation time
estimates: 41 bits of ms timestamp ≈ 69 years
10 bits machine id = 1,024 workers; 12 bits sequence = 4,096 IDs/ms per worker
api: nextId() → int64 (in-process library or tiny service)
dataModel: Layout: 1 sign | 41 timestamp ms since custom epoch | 5 DC | 5 worker | 12 sequence
Worker ids leased from ZooKeeper/etcd or config
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S1["Service A"] --> G1["ID worker 1"]
  S2["Service B"] --> G2["ID worker 2"]
  G1 -. "lease worker id" .-> Z[("etcd / ZooKeeper")]
  G2 -. "lease worker id" .-> Z
  G1 --> T["timestamp | dc | worker | seq"]

deepDives.title: Options
deepDives.body: DB auto-increment is simple but a bottleneck and leaks volume. Ticket servers (Flickr) use two DBs with odd/even IDs. UUIDv4 needs no coordination but is 128-bit and random, hurting B-tree locality. UUIDv7/ULID add a time prefix. Snowflake fits 64 bits and sorts by time.

deepDives.title: Clock problems
deepDives.body: If NTP moves the clock backwards, a worker could reissue IDs. Detect it and wait (or refuse) until time passes the last issued timestamp.

deepDives.title: Sequence overflow
deepDives.body: More than 4,096 IDs in one millisecond: spin until the next millisecond.

tradeoffs: 64-bit compactness vs coordination for worker ids
Time-ordering vs leaking creation time and volume
Random UUIDs vs index locality
probes: Why not just use UUIDv4?
What happens if the clock goes backwards?
How are worker ids assigned and reclaimed?

cases.title: Notification system
cases.summary: Send push, SMS and email reliably at scale while respecting user preferences.
functional: Services send notifications to users over push, SMS and email
Users choose channels and quiet hours
nonFunctional: Soft real-time: < 5 s for transactional messages
estimates: 10M push + 1M SMS + 5M email per day ≈ 200 msgs/s average, bursts of 50k/s for campaigns
dataModel: preferences(user_id, channel, enabled, quiet_hours)
devices(user_id, token, platform)
notification_log(id, user_id, channel, status, attempts) for dedup and audit
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SVC["Product services"] --> API["Notification API"]
  API --> P[("Prefs + templates")]
  API --> Q["Queue per channel"]
  Q --> WP["Push workers"] --> APNS["APNs / FCM"]
  Q --> WS["SMS workers"] --> TW["SMS provider"]
  Q --> WE["Email workers"] --> SES["Email provider"]
  WP --> LOG[("Delivery log")]
  WS --> LOG
  WE --> LOG
  Q --> DLQ["Dead-letter queue"]

deepDives.title: Decoupling by channel
deepDives.body: One queue per channel isolates failures: an SMS provider outage doesn't stall push. Workers scale independently.

deepDives.title: Retries and dedup
deepDives.body: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; after N attempts park the message in a DLQ. An idempotency key + delivery log stops duplicates when a worker crashes after sending.

deepDives.title: Preferences and rate limits
deepDives.body: Check opt-outs and quiet hours before enqueueing; cap per-user frequency so a bug can't spam people.

tradeoffs: At-least-once + dedup vs exactly-once (not really achievable end to end)
Fan-out at send time vs per-segment batch jobs
Single vs multiple providers per channel
probes: How do you avoid sending the same push twice?
What happens when APNs is down for an hour?
How do you send to 50M users in a campaign?

readings.title: AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter
AWS Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

cases.title: News feed (Twitter / Instagram)
cases.summary: Build each user's home timeline from the people they follow, fast.
functional: Home timeline of followed users' posts, newest or ranked
nonFunctional: New posts visible to followers within ~5 s
estimates: 300M DAU × 5 timeline loads = 1.5B reads/day ≈ 17k/s, peak 50k/s
50M posts/day ≈ 600 writes/s; average 200 followers → 120k timeline inserts/s with fan-out on write
dataModel: posts(post_id snowflake, author_id, text, media, created_at) sharded by author
follows(follower_id, followee_id) both directions
timeline cache: Redis list of post ids per user (last ~800)
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Client"] --> API["API gateway"]
  API --> PS["Post service"] --> PDB[("Posts DB")]
  PS --> K["Kafka: new posts"]
  K --> FO["Fan-out workers"]
  FO --> G[("Follow graph")]
  FO --> TC[("Timeline cache")]
  API --> TS["Timeline service"]
  TS --> TC
  TS -. "celebrity posts at read time" .-> PDB

deepDives.title: Fan-out on write vs read
deepDives.body: Push: on post, insert the id into every follower's cached timeline; reads are O(1) but writes explode for celebrities. Pull: build the timeline at read time by merging followees' recent posts; cheap writes, slow reads. Hybrid: push for normal users, pull celebrities' posts at read time and merge.

deepDives.title: Timeline cache
deepDives.body: Store only post ids in Redis lists, capped in length; hydrate post bodies from a post cache. Inactive users' timelines can be rebuilt on demand.

deepDives.title: Ranking
deepDives.body: Fetch a candidate set (a few hundred ids), score with a model (recency, affinity, engagement), and return the top N with a cursor.

tradeoffs: Write amplification vs read latency
Freshness vs cost for inactive users
Chronological simplicity vs ranked engagement
probes: What happens when someone with 100M followers posts?
How do you paginate a ranked feed without duplicates?
How do deletes propagate?

readings.title: Facebook TAO: the power of the graph

cases.title: Chat (WhatsApp / Slack)
cases.summary: 1:1 and group messaging with delivery receipts, offline sync and presence.
nonFunctional: Message delivery p99 < 500 ms when online
Hundreds of millions of concurrent connections
estimates: 100M DAU × 40 messages = 4B/day ≈ 46k msgs/s
100 B per message → 400 GB/day; years of history → PB scale
Each gateway holds ~500k WebSocket connections → ~200 gateways
api: WebSocket: send {chatId, clientMsgId, body} → ack {msgId, seq}
WebSocket push: message, receipt, presence events
dataModel: messages(chat_id partition, seq clustering, sender, body, ts) in Cassandra/ScyllaDB
connection registry: user_id → gateway id (Redis)
per-device last-read seq
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A["Sender"] <--> GW1["WS gateway 1"]
  B["Recipient"] <--> GW2["WS gateway 2"]
  GW1 --> CS["Chat service"]
  CS --> DB[("Messages store")]
  CS --> REG[("Connection registry")]
  CS --> GW2
  CS -. offline .-> PN["Push notifications"]
  GW1 --> PR["Presence service"]

deepDives.title: Routing messages
deepDives.body: Gateways keep long-lived WebSockets. The chat service persists the message, assigns a per-chat sequence number, then looks up the recipient's gateway in the registry and forwards. If offline, send a push and let the client sync on reconnect.

deepDives.title: Ordering and dedup
deepDives.body: Clients send a clientMsgId; the server dedups retries and assigns a monotonic per-chat seq. Clients render by seq and fetch gaps.

deepDives.title: Storage
deepDives.body: Partition by chat id with seq as clustering key so a chat's history is one sequential read. Discord moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB for this access pattern.

deepDives.title: Presence
deepDives.body: Heartbeats every ~30 s update a TTL key; fan presence out only to contacts currently online, and batch it for large groups.

tradeoffs: WebSockets vs long-polling
Per-chat ordering vs global ordering
Storing on server vs end-to-end encryption limits
probes: How does a message find the right gateway?
How do you guarantee no loss if a gateway crashes?
How does a phone that was offline for a week catch up?

readings.title: Discord: How Discord stores trillions of messages

cases.title: Video streaming (YouTube / Netflix)
cases.summary: Upload, transcode and stream video worldwide with adaptive bitrate.
nonFunctional: Egress cost dominates: maximise CDN offload
estimates: 500 hours uploaded/min; 1 h ≈ 1-3 GB across renditions → ~1 PB/day new storage
1B views/day; egress handled almost entirely by CDN
dataModel: videos(id, owner, status, renditions[], duration)
raw + transcoded segments in object storage
view counts aggregated in a stream job
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Uploader"] -- "pre-signed URL" --> RAW[("Raw object store")]
  RAW --> Q["Transcode queue"]
  Q --> TW["Transcode workers"]
  TW --> SEG[("Segments store")]
  TW --> META[("Video metadata")]
  SEG --> CDN["CDN edge"]
  V["Viewer"] --> CDN
  V --> API["Playback API"] --> META

deepDives.title: Transcoding pipeline
deepDives.body: Split the upload into chunks, transcode chunks in parallel into a bitrate ladder (240p…4K, H.264/VP9/AV1), package into HLS/DASH segments of 2-6 s, then publish the manifest.

deepDives.title: Adaptive bitrate
deepDives.body: The player measures throughput and buffer and switches renditions segment by segment. Short segments adapt faster; long segments compress better.

deepDives.title: CDN strategy
deepDives.body: Popular titles are pre-positioned in ISP-embedded caches (Netflix Open Connect); the long tail is pulled on demand. View counts are batched client-side and aggregated asynchronously.

tradeoffs: More renditions vs storage/compute cost
Segment length: adaptivity vs efficiency
Pre-positioning vs pull-through caching
probes: Why chunk the transcode?
How does the player pick a bitrate?
How do you count views without hammering a DB?

cases.title: Ride hailing (Uber)
cases.summary: Match riders with nearby drivers in real time and track the trip.
functional: Drivers stream location every few seconds
Riders request a ride and get matched to a nearby driver
nonFunctional: Location ingest of millions of updates/s
Trip state must never be lost or double-assigned
estimates: 5M active drivers × 1 update/4 s ≈ 1.25M writes/s (in-memory only)
~100k ride requests/min at peak
dataModel: Location index: cell id (H3/geohash) → set of driver ids, in memory, sharded by region
trips(id, rider, driver, state, timestamps) in a strongly consistent DB
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D["Driver app"] --> LOC["Location service"]
  LOC --> GEO[("Geo index: H3 cells")]
  R["Rider app"] --> RS["Ride service"]
  RS --> M["Matching"]
  M --> GEO
  M -- offer --> D
  RS --> TRIP[("Trips DB")]
  RS --> PRICE["Pricing / surge"]

deepDives.title: Geo indexing
deepDives.body: Geohash prefixes, quadtrees or Uber's hexagonal H3 cells map a point to a cell; search the rider's cell plus neighbours (k-ring) for available drivers, then rank by ETA, not straight-line distance.

deepDives.title: Location ingest
deepDives.body: Updates are ephemeral: keep the latest position per driver in memory (sharded by city/cell), and stream to Kafka for analytics. Don't write every ping to a database.

deepDives.title: Matching without double-booking
deepDives.body: Offer to one driver at a time with a short timeout; claim the driver with a conditional update (driver.state = available → reserved) so two riders can't get the same driver.

tradeoffs: Hexagons (uniform neighbours) vs geohash (simple prefixes)
Greedy nearest match vs batch-optimised matching
In-memory speed vs durability for locations
probes: How do you find drivers within 2 km quickly?
How do you stop two riders getting one driver?
What's the trip state machine?

readings.title: H3: Uber's hexagonal hierarchical spatial index

cases.title: Payment system
cases.summary: Accept payments exactly once, keep a correct ledger and reconcile with providers.
functional: Charge a customer for an order via a payment provider
nonFunctional: Never charge twice; never lose money
estimates: 1M payments/day ≈ 12/s average: correctness, not throughput, is the hard part
api: POST /v1/payments {orderId, amount, currency, method} with Idempotency-Key
dataModel: payments(id, idempotency_key UNIQUE, order_id, status, provider_ref)
ledger_entries(id, txn_id, account, debit, credit) — every txn sums to zero
outbox table for events
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C["Checkout"] --> PAY["Payment service"]
  PAY --> DB[("Payments + ledger (SQL)")]
  PAY --> PSP["Payment provider"]
  PSP -- "signed webhook" --> WH["Webhook handler"]
  WH --> DB
  DB --> OUT["Outbox → Kafka"]
  REC["Reconciliation job"] --> DB
  REC --> PSP

deepDives.title: Idempotency
deepDives.body: The client sends an Idempotency-Key; the service stores it with the request hash and response. Retries return the stored result instead of charging again. Provider calls also pass an idempotency key.

deepDives.title: Double-entry ledger
deepDives.body: Every movement is a balanced set of debits and credits in one DB transaction; balances are derived, never edited in place. That makes errors detectable and audits possible.

deepDives.title: State and reconciliation
deepDives.body: Payment state machine (created → authorised → captured → refunded) updated by API responses and webhooks, whichever arrives first. A daily job reconciles the ledger against provider settlement files.

deepDives.title: Events
deepDives.body: Use the transactional outbox so 'payment captured' is published if and only if the DB commit happened.

tradeoffs: Synchronous capture vs async with webhooks
Strong consistency (SQL) vs availability
Build ledger vs buy
probes: The client timed out: did the charge happen?
How do you handle a webhook arriving before your API response?
How would you find a missing 1 rupee?

readings.title: Stripe: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
AWS Builders' Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs

cases.title: Ticket booking (BookMyShow / Ticketmaster)
cases.summary: Sell limited seats fairly under flash-sale load without overselling.
functional: Hold seats for a few minutes during checkout
Confirm after payment; release on timeout
nonFunctional: Survive 100× traffic spikes at on-sale time
estimates: Popular on-sale: 10M users for 50k seats in minutes → most requests must be absorbed before the DB
dataModel: seats(event_id, seat_id, status, hold_id, hold_expires_at) with conditional updates
holds(id, user_id, seat_ids, expires_at)
orders(id, hold_id, payment_id)
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Buyers"] --> WR["Virtual waiting room"]
  WR --> API["Booking API"]
  API --> INV[("Seat inventory (SQL)")]
  API --> H[("Holds with TTL")]
  API --> PAY["Payment service"]
  EXP["Expiry worker"] --> INV

deepDives.title: No overselling
deepDives.body: Reserve with an atomic conditional write: UPDATE seats SET status='held', hold_id=? WHERE seat_id IN (…) AND status='available'; succeed only if all rows changed. Optimistic concurrency beats long-held distributed locks.

deepDives.title: Holds with TTL
deepDives.body: A hold expires after ~10 minutes; a worker (or lazy check on read) releases expired holds. Payment confirmation flips held → sold only if the hold is still valid.

deepDives.title: Flash-sale protection
deepDives.body: A waiting room admits users at the rate the backend can handle and gives a fair queue position; static seat maps are served from CDN; the DB only sees admitted traffic.

tradeoffs: Pessimistic locks vs optimistic conditional updates
Hold length: conversion vs inventory locked up
Fairness vs throughput
probes: Two people click the same seat at once: who wins and how?
What if payment succeeds after the hold expired?
How do you protect the DB at on-sale time?

readings.title: Martin Kleppmann: How to do distributed locking
Shopify: Surviving flashes of high-write traffic
AWS Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload

cases.title: Collaborative editor (Google Docs)
cases.summary: Many people edit the same document in real time and converge on the same text.
nonFunctional: Edits visible to others in < 200 ms
All replicas converge to the same state
estimates: 10M DAU, ~10 editors per active doc, ~5 ops/s per active editor
api: WS /docs/{id}: send ops {clientId, seq, op}; receive transformed/merged ops
dataModel: ops log per doc (doc_id, version, op) append-only
periodic snapshots for fast load
presence in memory
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A["Editor A"] <--> S["Doc session server"]
  B["Editor B"] <--> S
  S --> OPS[("Ops log")]
  S --> SNAP[("Snapshots")]
  S --> PRES["Presence / cursors"]
  LB["Router: doc id → server"] --> S

deepDives.title: OT vs CRDT
deepDives.body: Operational transformation (Google Docs) needs a central server to order and transform concurrent ops. CRDTs (Yjs, Automerge) give each character a unique, ordered id so replicas merge without a central authority, which suits offline-first at the cost of metadata.

deepDives.title: One server per document
deepDives.body: Route all editors of a doc to the same session server (consistent hashing on doc id) so ordering is simple and state stays in memory; persist ops, snapshot periodically.

deepDives.title: History
deepDives.body: The append-only ops log plus snapshots give version history and undo for free.

tradeoffs: Central OT simplicity vs CRDT offline support
Snapshot frequency vs load time
Per-doc server affinity vs failover complexity
probes: Two users type at the same position: what happens?
How does an offline user's work merge?
How do you load a doc with a million edits quickly?

readings.title: Figma: Realtime editing of ordered sequences

cases.title: Search autocomplete (typeahead)
cases.summary: Suggest the top completions for a prefix as the user types.
functional: Return top 5-10 suggestions for a prefix
estimates: 10M DAU × 10 searches × ~6 keystrokes ≈ 600M requests/day ≈ 7k/s, peak 20k/s
dataModel: Trie where each node caches its top-K completions
Query logs → aggregated counts (daily/hourly)
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Search box"] --> CDN["CDN / browser cache"]
  CDN --> S["Suggest service"]
  S --> T[("In-memory trie with top-K")]
  LOGS["Query logs"] --> K["Kafka"]
  K --> AGG["Aggregation job"]
  AGG --> BUILD["Trie builder"]
  BUILD --> T

deepDives.title: Trie with cached top-K
deepDives.body: Walking a whole subtree per keystroke is too slow; store the top-K completions at every node so a lookup is O(prefix length).

deepDives.title: Building and updating
deepDives.body: Aggregate query counts offline (or in a stream with decay for trending), rebuild the trie periodically and swap it in atomically; shard by prefix range when it doesn't fit one machine.

deepDives.title: Client tricks
deepDives.body: Debounce keystrokes, cache responses per prefix in the browser and at the CDN, and filter offensive suggestions.

tradeoffs: Freshness vs rebuild cost
Global vs personalised suggestions
Memory per node (K) vs quality
probes: Why cache top-K at each trie node?
How do trending queries appear quickly?
How do you shard the trie?

readings.title: Facebook: The life of a typeahead query

cases.title: Web crawler
cases.summary: Crawl billions of pages politely, avoid duplicates and keep content fresh.
functional: Start from seed URLs and follow links
Re-crawl pages based on change rate
nonFunctional: Respect robots.txt and per-host rate limits
Robust to traps and malformed pages
estimates: 1B pages/month ≈ 400 pages/s; 100 KB each ≈ 100 TB/month raw
api: Internal: enqueue(url, priority); fetch workers pull by host
dataModel: URL frontier: priority queues + per-host queues
seen-URL set (Bloom filter + store)
content store keyed by URL hash; content fingerprints (simhash) for near-dup detection
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SEED["Seed URLs"] --> F["URL frontier"]
  F --> W["Fetch workers"]
  W --> DNS["DNS cache"]
  W --> RB["robots.txt cache"]
  W --> P["Parser"]
  P --> CS[("Content store")]
  P --> DD["URL dedup (Bloom)"]
  DD --> F

deepDives.title: Politeness
deepDives.body: Map each host to one queue served by one worker at a time with a delay between requests; cache robots.txt and DNS per host.

deepDives.title: Prioritisation and freshness
deepDives.body: Front queues by priority (PageRank-ish, change frequency), back queues by host. Re-crawl frequently changing pages more often.

deepDives.title: Dedup and traps
deepDives.body: Normalise URLs, check a Bloom filter before enqueueing, fingerprint content to skip mirrors, and cap depth/URL length to escape calendar-style traps.

tradeoffs: BFS breadth vs priority focus
Bloom filter false positives vs memory
Freshness vs crawl budget
probes: How do you avoid hammering one site?
How do you detect duplicate content at different URLs?
How do you scale the frontier across machines?

readings.title: Brin & Page: The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual web search engine

cases.title: File storage & sync (Dropbox)
cases.summary: Store files and keep them in sync across devices efficiently.
functional: Sync changes across a user's devices
estimates: 500M users × 2 GB average = 1 EB logical; dedup across users saves a lot
dataModel: blocks: content-addressed by SHA-256 in object storage
file_revisions(namespace, path, revision, block_list)
per-namespace journal for change cursors
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D["Desktop client"] --> MS["Metadata service"]
  D --> BS["Block service"]
  BS --> OBJ[("Block store")]
  MS --> MDB[("Metadata DB")]
  MS --> N["Notification service"]
  N -- "long-poll: changes" --> D2["Other devices"]
  D2 --> BS

deepDives.title: Chunking and dedup
deepDives.body: Split files into ~4 MB blocks identified by hash. Upload only blocks the server doesn't have, so edits and duplicates across users cost almost nothing.

deepDives.title: Metadata vs blocks
deepDives.body: Keep metadata (paths, revisions, block lists) in a strongly consistent DB; keep immutable blocks in cheap object storage. A commit atomically points a path at a new block list.

deepDives.title: Sync and conflicts
deepDives.body: Clients long-poll for changes after a cursor, then fetch new metadata and missing blocks. If two devices commit against the same base revision, keep both as a 'conflicted copy'.

tradeoffs: Block size: dedup granularity vs metadata overhead
Push notifications vs polling
Automatic merge vs conflicted copies
probes: How do you avoid re-uploading a 1 GB file after a 1-byte change?
How do other devices learn about the change?
How do you resolve offline conflicts?

readings.title: Dropbox: Rewriting the heart of our sync engine

cases.title: Ad click aggregator
cases.summary: Count billions of ad clicks per minute accurately for billing and dashboards.
functional: Aggregate clicks per ad per minute
Query counts for dashboards and billing
nonFunctional: Dashboard latency of a minute or two
estimates: 10B clicks/day ≈ 115k/s, peak 500k/s; 100 B each ≈ 1 TB/day raw
dataModel: Raw events in Kafka (partitioned by adId) and cold storage
Aggregates (ad_id, minute, count) in an OLAP store (Druid/ClickHouse/Pinot)
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Click"] --> T["Click tracker"]
  T --> K["Kafka: raw clicks"]
  K --> SP["Stream processor (Flink)"]
  SP --> OLAP[("OLAP store")]
  K --> RAW[("Raw archive")]
  RAW --> BATCH["Daily batch recompute"]
  BATCH --> OLAP
  DASH["Dashboards / billing"] --> OLAP

deepDives.title: Windows and late data
deepDives.body: Tumbling one-minute windows keyed by adId in event time; watermarks decide when a window closes and allowed lateness lets stragglers update it.

deepDives.title: Exactly-once counting
deepDives.body: Dedup by clickId within a window, and use Flink checkpoints with transactional sinks (or idempotent upserts keyed by ad+minute) so replays don't double count.

deepDives.title: Lambda vs Kappa
deepDives.body: Lambda runs a batch path for truth plus a speed path for freshness (two codebases). Kappa replays the log through one streaming job when logic changes. A daily reconciliation batch is common for billing.

deepDives.title: Hot ads
deepDives.body: A viral ad overloads one partition: pre-aggregate locally or salt the key (adId#n) and merge.

tradeoffs: Freshness vs accuracy
Lambda (two paths) vs Kappa (replay)
Raw retention cost vs reprocessing ability
probes: How do you avoid double counting on retries?
What do you do with events that arrive 10 minutes late?
How would you recompute a day after fixing a bug?

readings.title: Jay Kreps: Questioning the Lambda architecture

cases.title: Real-time leaderboard
cases.summary: Rank millions of players by score with instant rank lookups.
functional: A player's own rank and neighbours
nonFunctional: Score updates visible within a second
estimates: 10M players; 5k score updates/s; sorted set of 10M members ≈ 1 GB in Redis
dataModel: Redis sorted set per leaderboard/season: ZINCRBY, ZREVRANGE, ZREVRANK
Durable score history in a DB for rebuilds and audit
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  G["Game servers"] --> S["Score service"]
  S --> Z[("Redis sorted sets")]
  S --> DB[("Scores DB")]
  P["Players"] --> API["Leaderboard API"]
  API --> Z

deepDives.title: Sorted sets
deepDives.body: A skip-list-backed sorted set gives O(log n) updates and rank queries, and top-N via range reads.

deepDives.title: Scaling beyond one node
deepDives.body: Shard by score range or by region and merge top-N from shards; for approximate global ranks, use score buckets (histogram) to estimate percentile.

deepDives.title: Durability
deepDives.body: Redis holds the hot view; write scores to a DB (or stream) as the source of truth so the sorted set can be rebuilt.

tradeoffs: Exact rank (single sorted set) vs approximate at huge scale
Real-time vs periodic snapshots
Memory cost of many leaderboards
probes: How do you get a player's exact rank among 100M?
How do ties work?
How do you reset weekly boards?
